weekLabel: Week 6 · Meeting A · Visual Reasoning: Static and Dynamic Evidence

slides.title: See the evidence, don't just compute it
slides.subtitle: Matching a question to an encoding, the fig/ax pattern, labeled and annotated static figures, and animated .gif evidence
slides.teaching: Open by asking: if South-zone rooms really do use about 80% more energy than North (Week 5's finding), how would you convince someone who will never read a groupby table? Preview that today builds the chart -- and the animation -- that make that claim visible.

slides.title: A chart is an answer to a question, not decoration
slides.statement: Every figure should be built to answer one specific question -- distribution, comparison, relationship, or change over a sequence -- not just "let's plot this and see."
slides.supporting: Static figures and one dynamic .gif are two co-equal forms of evidence this week -- not a required chart plus an optional animated extra.
slides.teaching: Emphasize 'co-equal' explicitly here -- this framing recurs at the FuncAnimation section later and should not be treated as a late addendum tacked onto static charts.

outcomes.head: Match
outcomes.body: Choose the right chart encoding (distribution / comparison / relationship / change-over-time) for a stated question.

outcomes.head: Build
outcomes.body: Use the fig, ax pattern to build a figure with every axis labeled, its unit stated, and a legend when more than one series is plotted.

outcomes.head: Annotate
outcomes.body: Annotate one outlier or turning point directly on a figure using ax.annotate, instead of only describing it in a caption.

outcomes.head: Animate
outcomes.body: Build a matplotlib.animation.FuncAnimation and save it as a shareable .gif.

slides.teaching: Flag outcome 4 explicitly as equal in weight to outcomes 1-3, not a bonus -- this is the framing the whole session protects.

items: The fig, ax pattern, labeled and legended
Annotate an outlier -- don't just caption it
Dynamic evidence: FuncAnimation, saved as a .gif
slides.teaching: Tell students today's four Radley Hall figures (one per agenda item) are the full menu of encodings; Project 1 Part III asks for exactly two of these -- a group/distribution figure and a relationship/change figure -- on their own dataset, with today's .gif available as one path through Part IV's evidence extension.

slides.title: Visual encoding, defined
slides.definition: The mapping from a data value to a visual property -- position on an axis, bar height, marker position, color. Different questions call for different encodings; the encoding should follow the question, not the other way around.

example.head: Four question families
example.body:
Distribution: how is one variable spread out?
Comparison: how do groups differ?
Relationship: do two variables move together?
Change over a sequence: how does a value move across an order (time, floor, iteration).

slides.teaching: Write the four question families on the board before any chart type is named -- the point is that the question comes first, the chart type is chosen in service of it.

slides.title: Match each question family to a chart encoding
rows: How is energy use spread across all rooms?
How do North and South zones differ?
Does room area move together with energy use?
How does a value move across an order?
slides.callout: Pick the encoding after the question, not before -- a bar chart cannot show a relationship, and a scatter plot cannot show one group's total.
slides.teaching: Walk the four rows left to right. Ask students to name which row's chart type could NOT answer one of the other rows' questions -- the point is the encodings are not interchangeable.

slides.title: fig, ax -- defined
slides.definition: fig, ax = plt.subplots() creates two objects in one line. fig is the whole figure -- the canvas and everything on it. ax is one set of axes -- the actual plot area, with its own data, ticks, and labels. Nearly every call after this line is a method on ax, not on fig.

example.head: Why keep both names
example.body: One fig can later hold several ax panels (a grid of subplots). Naming both objects explicitly -- instead of trusting a hidden 'current plot' -- is exactly what lets you label, legend, annotate, and save the specific figure you built.

slides.teaching: Contrast with plt.plot() used alone (no named ax) -- explain that this course always names fig and ax because later slides need to call methods on a specific ax.

slides.title: Two objects, one line: fig, ax = plt.subplots()
slides.code:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot([1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6])

fig.savefig("first_plot.png")
slides.explainBody: plt.subplots() returns fig and ax together. ax.plot() draws a line through three points -- a method call on ax, not a free-floating plt.plot(). fig.savefig() writes the picture straight to a file; the figure does not need to be displayed on screen to be saved.
slides.teaching: Run this live and open first_plot.png from the Files pane -- some students expect a pop-up window; explain that scripted Matplotlib in Spyder does not require one to produce a saved file.

slides.title: Predict: how many numbers come back in edges?
slides.code:
energy = df["energy_kwh_m2_yr"].dropna()

counts, edges = np.histogram(energy, bins=6)
print(len(counts))
print(len(edges))
slides.question: How many numbers does edges contain?
options: 7 -- one more edge than bins (edges mark boundaries, including both ends)
23 -- one edge per room in the dataset
5 -- one fewer than the bin count
slides.why: Verified: 6 bins need 7 boundary edges -- edges always has one more entry than counts.
slides.teaching: Ask students to sketch 3 bins on the board first and count the boundary marks between and around them (4) before revealing this is the same off-by-one logic scaled up to 6 bins.

slides.title: A histogram counts, before it ever draws
slides.code:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv("building_rooms.csv")
energy = df["energy_kwh_m2_yr"].dropna()

counts, edges = np.histogram(energy, bins=6)
print(counts)
print(np.round(edges, 1))
slides.explainHead: Four empty bins is real evidence, not a bug
slides.explainBody: .dropna() drops the one room (R206) with no recorded energy value -- the same gap Week 4's trustworthiness interview flagged -- before np.histogram ever sees the data. np.histogram then splits the remaining 23 rooms' range into 6 equal-width bins and counts how many fall in each -- before any bar is ever drawn. One extreme value (room R306, 410.0 kWh/m2/yr) stretches the whole axis, compressing the other 22 rooms into just the first two bins.
slides.teaching: Ask students to guess, before revealing edges, how wide each bin must be if the axis has to stretch from 12 all the way to 410 in only 6 equal steps. Confirm len(edges) is 7, exactly as the previous slide predicted.

slides.title: Distribution: room energy use, six bins
slides.chartTitle: Distribution of room energy use, Radley Hall
slides.explainBody: Six bars, one per bin computed on the previous slide. Most rooms cluster in the first two bins (12-145 kWh/m2/yr); the lone bar at far right is room R306 alone -- exactly the outlier Week 5's IQR and z-score rules both flagged.
slides.teaching: Point out this is a real, rendered chart -- not a description of one. Ask what a reader would wrongly assume about 'typical' energy use if the R306 bar were quietly dropped.

slides.title: ax.hist() does the same calculation, then draws it
slides.code:
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4))
ax.hist(df["energy_kwh_m2_yr"].dropna(), bins=6,
        color="#3D8DFF", edgecolor="white")

ax.set_xlabel("Energy use intensity (kWh/m2/yr)")
ax.set_ylabel("Number of rooms")
ax.set_title("Distribution of room energy use, Radley Hall")

fig.savefig("energy_distribution.png")
slides.explainHead: Label every axis, always with a unit
slides.explainBody: This produces the exact bar chart from the previous slide, built from real Matplotlib rather than a pre-computed count. ax.hist() runs the same np.histogram calculation internally. An axis of bare numbers with no unit is not evidence -- always name what each axis measures before saving.
slides.teaching: Have students identify, out loud, the three separate calls that make this a defensible figure: hist(), set_xlabel()/set_ylabel(), and set_title() -- three habits, not one.

slides.title: Labeled axes, defined
slides.definition: Names what the x-axis measures; ax.set_ylabel() does the same for the y-axis. Always include the unit (m2, kWh/m2/yr), and do this before fig.savefig(), not after: a saved image file cannot be relabeled without rerunning the code.

example.head: Why the unit matters
example.body: An axis labeled only 'Energy' (no unit) actually claims what -- kWh total? per m2? per year? An unlabeled unit is a real ambiguity, not a cosmetic gap.

slides.teaching: Ask what an axis labeled only 'Energy' (no unit) actually claims -- kWh total? per m2? per year? An unlabeled unit is a real ambiguity, not a cosmetic gap.

slides.title: Legend, defined
slides.definition: Draws a key matching each color or marker to its label. Required whenever a figure plots more than one labeled series -- for example, North rooms in one color and South rooms in another on the same axes.

example.head: When it's required
example.body: Any time more than one labeled series shares one set of axes -- for example, North rooms in one color and South rooms in another on the same scatter plot, coming up shortly.

slides.teaching: A legend is required, not optional, the moment a figure plots two labeled series on the same axes -- point to the upcoming North/South scatter as the exact case.

slides.title: Predict: what does zone_summary actually print?
slides.code:
zone_summary = df.groupby("zone").agg(
    mean_energy=("energy_kwh_m2_yr", "mean"),
    mean_area=("area_m2", "mean"),
    n=("room_id", "count"),
).round(2)
print(zone_summary)
slides.question: What does print(zone_summary) actually show?
options: zone as a normal column, plus mean_energy/mean_area/n, on a default integer index
zone as the index label (not a column); mean_energy, mean_area, n as the columns
A single Series named zone, one number per zone
A GroupBy object -- .agg() hasn't actually run yet
slides.why: Verified: zone became the index (zone_summary.index.name == 'zone'), not a column -- zone_summary['zone'] raises KeyError.
slides.teaching: This is the single most common mix-up when a student later tries zone_summary['zone'] and hits a KeyError -- flag it now, before it happens live in Meeting B.

slides.title: Recall Week 5's headline finding
slides.code:
zone_summary = df.groupby("zone").agg(
    mean_energy=("energy_kwh_m2_yr", "mean"),
    mean_area=("area_m2", "mean"),
    n=("room_id", "count"),
).round(2)
print(zone_summary)
slides.output:
mean_energy  mean_area   n
zone                             
North        64.25      40.98  12
South       115.68      38.25  12
slides.explainHead: Same finding as Week 5 -- now make it visible
slides.explainBody: South-zone rooms average 115.68 kWh/m2/yr against North's 64.25 -- about 80% higher -- despite nearly identical average area and identical room counts. zone sits in the index, exactly as the previous slide predicted. The next two slides turn this one row into an unmissable visual claim.
slides.teaching: This is a direct reuse of Week 5's exact numbers -- do not recompute or re-derive them here; the point of today is visualizing an already-established finding.

slides.title: Comparison: one bar per group, drawn from that table
slides.code:
zone_energy = df.groupby("zone")["energy_kwh_m2_yr"].mean().round(2)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4))
ax.bar(zone_energy.index, zone_energy.values, color="#3D8DFF")

ax.set_xlabel("Zone")
ax.set_ylabel("Mean energy use intensity (kWh/m2/yr)")
ax.set_title("North vs. South zone energy use, Radley Hall")

fig.savefig("zone_comparison.png")
slides.explainHead: A height difference a reader sees in one second
slides.explainBody: zone_energy is a two-row Series -- one mean per zone. ax.bar() draws one bar per index label. The gap between North and South is now something a reader sees immediately, instead of comparing two numbers in a table.
slides.teaching: Ask why this chart alone, without the earlier table, would still be defensible evidence -- the n=12/12 sample-size context from Week 5 is the piece a chart like this can silently lose if it's shown without its source table nearby.

slides.title: Comparison: North vs. South, visualized
slides.chartTitle: North vs. South zone energy use, Radley Hall
slides.explainBody: Same two numbers as the recall slide, now a chart instead of a table row. This is the shape of figure Project 1 Part III's required comparison figure should produce for your own dataset's own grouping variable.
slides.teaching: Ask what's missing from this chart that the earlier table had -- the answer is n (sample size per group); a bar chart of means alone can hide a small, unreliable sample.

slides.title: Annotation, defined
slides.definition: ax.annotate(text, xy=(x, y), xytext=(x2, y2)) draws a text label pointing at one specific data point. xy is the point being pointed AT; xytext is where the text box itself sits; arrowprops draws the connecting arrow.

example.head: Why annotate one point
example.body: A figure caption cannot say 'the dot in the far corner is unusual' as clearly as an arrow pointing directly at it. Annotate the outlier or turning point on the figure itself, so the claim survives even if the caption is never read.

slides.note: xy is the point pointed AT. xytext is where the label itself sits. Swapping the two is the single most common mistake with ax.annotate() -- it does not error, it just points the arrow at the wrong place.
slides.teaching: Write xy and xytext on the board as two separate coordinate pairs before showing code -- the single most common student mix-up is swapping which one is which.

slides.title: Relationship: one chart, three questions answered
slides.code:
has_energy = df["energy_kwh_m2_yr"].notna()
north = df[has_energy & (df["zone"] == "North")]
south = df[has_energy & (df["zone"] == "South")]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4.5))
ax.scatter(north["area_m2"], north["energy_kwh_m2_yr"], color="#3D8DFF", label="North")
ax.scatter(south["area_m2"], south["energy_kwh_m2_yr"], color="#C9473A", label="South")
ax.annotate("R306: 410.0 kWh/m2/yr", xy=(8.0, 410.0), xytext=(52, 400), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->"))
ax.annotate("R309: 68.0 kWh/m2/yr", xy=(120.0, 68.0), xytext=(70, 180), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->"))
ax.set_xlabel("Room area (m2)")
ax.set_ylabel("Energy (kWh/m2/yr)")
ax.legend(loc="lower right")
fig.savefig("area_vs_energy.png")
slides.explainHead: Color, position, and two arrows -- one figure
slides.explainBody: has_energy & (df["zone"] == "North") reuses Week 5's &/| rule for combining two Boolean Series -- & instead of and, with parentheses around each comparison because & binds tighter than ==. The color answers "which zone?" -- a comparison folded into a relationship chart. Two ax.annotate() calls label the two rooms Week 5 flagged by different rules: R306 (both rules agreed) and R309 (only z-score flagged it, on area_m2). No single table cell does all three jobs at once.
slides.teaching: Point out south is n=11, not 12 -- room R206's missing energy value is dropped here, the same missing value from Week 4's trustworthiness interview. Note also this is the SAME area_m2/energy relationship Week 5 discussed only as numbers -- today it becomes a picture.

slides.title: Relationship: area vs. energy, all 23 rooms
slides.chartTitle: Area vs. energy use, all 23 measured rooms
slides.explainHead: The raw relationship, before color and annotation
slides.explainBody: A native chart shows this shape fast -- one clear high point at low area, room R306. But it cannot color points by zone or annotate one point with an arrow and caption the way the Matplotlib code on the previous slide can. That gap is exactly why this course teaches Matplotlib code, not only a spreadsheet chart tool.
slides.teaching: Use this contrast deliberately -- name out loud that a fast native chart is a legitimate first look, but the annotated, submittable evidence Project 1 requires needs the code version.

slides.title: The fourth question family: change over a sequence

left.head: What it asks
left.body: Distribution, comparison, and relationship all describe ONE snapshot of the data. The fourth family asks how a value moves across an order -- time, an iteration count, or (with no date column in Radley Hall) an ordered category like floor.

right.head: Line chart, the usual encoding
right.body: A line chart connects points in sequence order, so a reader's eye follows the trend instead of comparing isolated bars. Radley Hall has no date column, so today's example orders by floor (1, 2, 3) instead of by time.

slides.teaching: Be explicit that a line chart implies an ORDER, not just a category -- reordering North/South alphabetically would be fine for a bar chart, but reordering floors 3,1,2 on a line chart would misrepresent the sequence.

slides.title: Change over a sequence: mean energy by floor
slides.code:
by_floor = df.groupby("floor")["energy_kwh_m2_yr"].mean().round(2)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4))
ax.plot(by_floor.index, by_floor.values, marker="o", color="#3D8DFF")
ax.set_xlabel("Floor")
ax.set_ylabel("Mean energy use intensity (kWh/m2/yr)")
ax.set_title("Mean energy use by floor, Radley Hall")
ax.set_xticks([1, 2, 3])
ax.annotate("Floor 3 includes R306\n(410.0 kWh/m2/yr)",
            xy=(3, 113.61), xytext=(1.3, 100),
            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->"))
fig.savefig("floor_trend.png")
slides.explainHead: A rising line -- but check what's inside it
slides.explainBody: Energy use rises from floor 1 (66.29) to floor 3 (113.61). But floor 3 also contains room R306, the 410.0 kWh/m2/yr outlier, among only 9 rooms. Annotate that fact directly rather than letting the line imply every floor-3 room simply runs hotter.
slides.teaching: This is a genuine open question, not a solved one -- ask whether the class believes 'higher floors use more energy' or 'floor 3 happens to contain one server closet' is the better-supported claim from this data alone.

slides.title: Change over a sequence: energy by floor
slides.chartTitle: Mean energy use by floor, Radley Hall
slides.explainHead: A trend, with one honest caveat
slides.explainBody: 66.29 to 79.57 to 113.61 -- energy use does climb by floor. But floor 3 has only 9 rooms and includes R306; do not present this line as 'every higher floor runs hotter' without naming that one room's outsized share of the floor-3 average.
slides.teaching: Contrast this chart with the earlier bar chart -- ask why a line, not bars, is the right choice here (floor has a genuine order; zone North/South does not).

slides.title: FuncAnimation, defined
slides.definition: matplotlib.animation.FuncAnimation(fig, update, frames=n) calls your own update(frame) function once per frame, each time redrawing ax with that frame's slice of the data -- the animation equivalent of a for loop over frames.

example.head: The animation equivalent of a loop
example.body: Everything shown so far in this deck was a snapshot. FuncAnimation is the first tool this course has taught that shows a claim CHANGING, frame by frame, instead of stated once.

slides.teaching: Say plainly: everything in the last several slides was a snapshot. This is the first tool this course has taught that shows a claim CHANGING, not just stated once.

slides.title: frame, defined
slides.definition: One still image in the sequence -- frame 0 is drawn first, frame 1 second, and so on. Each frame calls your update(frame) function once, with that frame's number passed in.

example.head: Saving every frame as one file
example.body: ani.save(path, writer="pillow") stitches every frame into one shareable .gif file; no live window is required to produce it.

slides.teaching: Confirm students can say, in one sentence, the difference between a frame (one still image) and the saved .gif (every frame stitched together).

slides.title: Anatomy of a FuncAnimation(...) call

parts.label: Stores the animation
parts.body: Keeps a reference so ani.save(...) can be called after this line.

parts.label: The constructor
parts.body: Builds the animation from one fig and a per-frame update function.

parts.label: The figure
parts.body: The one fig created once with plt.subplots(), reused every frame.

parts.label: Frame updater
parts.body: Called once per frame, as update(frame); redraws ax each time.

parts.label: Frame count
parts.body: update is called once per frame, for frame = 0, 1, ... n-1.

slides.teaching: Point to each numbered chip in order -- ani is the object saved later; FuncAnimation is the constructor; fig is the figure reused every frame; update is the function called once per frame; frames=n sets how many times update runs.

slides.title: Four moves build any FuncAnimation

steps.label: SET UP
steps.head: Create fig, ax once
steps.body: Build the figure and axes outside the loop -- they get reused every frame, not recreated.

steps.label: UPDATE
steps.head: Write update(frame)
steps.body: Clear ax, redraw using only data through this frame, then reset labels, limits, and title -- ax.clear() erases them too.

steps.label: ANIMATE
steps.head: Call FuncAnimation
steps.body: Pass the figure, the update function, and how many frames to run.

steps.label: SAVE
steps.head: Save as a .gif
steps.body: ani.save(path, writer="pillow") writes every frame to one shareable file -- no live window needed.

slides.teaching: Walk this exactly in order on the board before showing any code -- students should be able to name all four moves from memory before Meeting B's studio.

slides.title: Predict: what happens without ax.set_ylim() in update()?
slides.code:
def update(frame):
    ax.clear()
    shown = plot_df.iloc[: frame + 1]
    ax.bar(shown["room_id"],
           shown["energy_kwh_m2_yr"])
slides.question: What happens to the y-axis across frames, with no ax.set_ylim()?
options: Stays fixed at 0-430 -- matplotlib remembers the original scale
Autorescales to fit only the bars shown so far -- early bars can look as tall as R306's
FuncAnimation errors -- limits must be set once outside update()
Old bars stay drawn on top, since ax.clear() removes labels but not bars
slides.why: Verified: ax.clear() wipes stored limits; each new bar() autoscales y to that frame's own max value, not a fixed scale.
slides.teaching: Let students commit to an answer before revealing -- most beginners assume matplotlib 'remembers' a scale once set; ax.clear() erasing stored limits, not just drawn artists, is the point of this check.

slides.title: 23 frames, one room revealed at a time
slides.code:
import matplotlib.animation as animation
plot_df = df.dropna(subset=["energy_kwh_m2_yr"]).sort_values("energy_kwh_m2_yr").reset_index(drop=True)
n = len(plot_df)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))
def update(frame):
    ax.clear()
    shown = plot_df.iloc[: frame + 1]
    ax.bar(shown["room_id"], shown["energy_kwh_m2_yr"])
    ax.set_xlim(-0.5, n - 0.5)
    ax.set_ylim(0, 430)
    ax.set_xlabel("Room (sorted low to high)")
    ax.set_ylabel("Energy (kWh/m2/yr)")
    ax.set_title(f"{frame + 1} of {n} rooms")
ani = animation.FuncAnimation(fig, update, frames=n)
slides.explainHead: Nothing is animated yet -- only assembled
slides.explainBody: Frame 0 shows only the lowest-energy room; each later frame adds one more bar, in ascending order, until frame 22 shows all 23 rooms with R306's tall bar arriving last. set_xlim/set_ylim are re-set every frame -- exactly the two lines the previous predict removed -- so bar heights stay comparable across frames.
slides.teaching: Point at ax.clear() and ask what would happen without it (bars from every previous frame would pile up rather than being redrawn cleanly) -- this is the single most common animation bug.

slides.title: Save the sequence as one shareable .gif
slides.code:
import matplotlib.animation as animation

ani.save("energy_reporting.gif", writer="pillow", fps=5)
slides.explainHead: One file, playable anywhere, no Python required to view it
slides.explainBody: ani.save() renders every one of the 23 frames and writes them into a single .gif using the Pillow writer (installed alongside Matplotlib). No plt.show() call is needed -- check the Files pane in Spyder for energy_reporting.gif once this cell finishes running. This is the deliverable a caption should accompany, not a lecture-only demo.
slides.teaching: Confirm out loud that this .gif is graded with the exact same weight as the three static figures on the earlier slides -- restate the co-equal framing from the very start of this deck.

slides.title: Static and dynamic are two forms of evidence, not one primary and one extra
slides.statement: A static figure shows a finished claim. A .gif shows how that claim was built, room by room -- this week teaches both with equal depth and equal rigor.
slides.supporting: Project 1 Part III needs exactly two static figures, built with today's fig, ax pattern. Part IV then asks you to choose ONE evidence extension -- a FuncAnimation .gif (this week) or a GeoPandas map (Week 7) -- not both, and not neither.
slides.teaching: Correct two beliefs at once before Meeting B's studio begins: it is not four figures (Part III needs exactly two), and the gif is not automatically required either -- it is one of two legitimate Part IV choices, alongside next week's GeoPandas map. Build the animation skill for real regardless; many students will choose it.

slides.title: Transfer the encoding: four architectural questions
slides.prompt: Choose the visual form from the decision question—not from habit. No code required.
steps: Room-area spread → choose a distribution view and label m².
Embodied carbon by assembly → choose a comparison view and label kgCO₂e.
WWR versus simulated EUI → choose a relationship view and identify a useful annotation.
Monthly overheating hours → choose a change-over-time view and state whether animation adds evidence.
slides.teaching: Expected: histogram for room-area distribution; bar chart for carbon by assembly; scatterplot for WWR–EUI relationship; line plot for monthly overheating. Animation is justified only if the sequence itself reveals an accumulation or transition that a static line cannot. Require one reason, unit, and honest annotation for every answer.

slides.title: A current visualization workflow separates evidence from delivery

steps.label: QUESTION
steps.head: Name the comparison
steps.body: Distribution, comparison, relationship, change, spatial pattern, or uncertainty comes before a chart type.

steps.label: SPECIFY
steps.head: Make the view reproducible
steps.body: Code or a declarative specification should rebuild the same encodings, filters, labels, and scales.

steps.label: ACCESS
steps.head: Do not rely on color alone
steps.body: Use direct labels, sufficient contrast, and a concise description of the chart's structure and finding.

steps.label: DELIVER
steps.head: Choose the lightest useful medium
steps.body: Prefer static for a fixed claim; animate sequence; add interaction only when exploration changes the answer.

slides.teaching: Optional current-practice bridge. Name Vega-Lite as one declarative example without changing today's Matplotlib core. The professional habit is the sequence: question → reproducible specification → accessible encoding → justified delivery medium. Ask students which step an AI-generated chart most often skips; expected answer: the question or the accessibility check.

slides.title: Four questions, four encodings, one honest annotation
takeaways: Pick the encoding from the question -- distribution, comparison, relationship, or change over a sequence.
fig, ax names the canvas and the plot area explicitly -- label every axis with its unit.
Annotate the one outlier or turning point that matters, directly on the figure.
A .gif built with FuncAnimation is real, gradable evidence -- Project 1 Part IV lets you choose it, or next week's GeoPandas map, as your one evidence extension.
slides.teaching: Exit prompt: ask students which of today's four Radley Hall figures they would open a design conversation with, and why that one over the other three.
